title: Lock a used safety needle's hinged sheath one-handed by pressing it on the table, then put the syringe in a sharps tray
instruction: Lock the used needle's safety sheath by pressing it on the table with the holding hand, then put the syringe in the sharps tray.
context: Giving injections is core work for medical assistants (O*NET 31-9092.00: 'Prepare and administer medications as directed by a physician'; about 0.8 million US jobs), registered nurses (29-1141.00: 'Administer medications to patients and monitor patients for reactions or side effects'; 3.3 million) and licensed practical nurses (29-2061.00: 'Administer prescribed medications or start intravenous fluids'; 0.6 million). Every injection ends the same way: the worker shields the safety needle at once with the hand that holds the syringe and drops it in the sharps container. The maker of this hinged-sheath needle (Terumo SurGuard 3) gives three one-handed ways: finger, thumb, or pressing the sheath on a hard surface until it clicks. Needlesticks happen when the other hand comes near the point. Physically, the holding hand pinches a 10.5 mm barrel and must swing a 42 mm sheath through 100 deg, then snap its catch over a 0.5 mm needle, using only the table's reaction of a few newtons.
setup:
Metres; world x forward, y left, z up; origin midway between the arm bases (0,+/-0.305,0.750); table top z=0.7475. The table is the firm surface (rigid laminate). All items start at rest.
(1) Syringe with safety needle, free, 7.05 g: a 3 mL hypodermic syringe with a hinged-sheath safety needle, 25 G x 1 in (Terumo SurGuard 3 class, e.g. SG3-03L2525). Polypropylene barrel 10.5 mm outside diameter, 66 mm long; finger flange 22 mm wide; plunger pushed fully in, thumb rest 12 mm behind the flange; needle hub 20 mm long (6.4 mm collar, 4.4 mm nose); steel cannula 0.5 mm across, 25 mm long; 123 mm overall. It has just been laid down beside the pad after the injection (so every trial starts from the same pose; a worker would usually shield it straight from the injection grip) and lies on its side with the barrel axis along y at (0.230, -0.040), axis 5.25 mm above the table, needle pointing to -y (tip at y=-0.115), plunger end at y=+0.008, 70 mm from the pad's nearest edge.
(2) Safety sheath, part of (1), 0.6 g: an orange polypropylene U-channel 42 mm long, 9 mm wide, 8.5 mm deep with 1 mm walls (inside 7 mm wide, 7.5 mm deep), hinged on a pin on the hub collar 4 mm off the needle axis, 6 mm behind the front of the hub. It starts open at 100 deg from the needle, sticking out level toward the robot (-x), its far end at about (0.185, -0.077). The hinge's friction holds it where it is put: 0.012 N m (0.3 N at its end) and closes around the needle: closed, the needle lies on the channel's centre line, 3.5 mm from the walls, its tip 11 mm inside the far end. A hard stop is 3 deg past closed.
(3) Catch, inside the sheath: a sprung plunger in one side wall, 25 mm from the hinge pin, with a 1.5 mm round nose that reaches 0.2 mm past the needle's centre line and a square heel. Spring 600 N/m preloaded to 3.0 N, 1.2 mm travel. In the last 8 deg of closing the needle lifts the nose 0.44 mm against the spring and passes; the catch drops back behind the needle with a click, and the square heel then keeps the sheath within 1 deg of closed. Force to click, pressed at the sheath's far end: about 3 N, the low end of the 3 to 6 N we estimate for a real unit (the maker publishes no figure; 2.4 to 3.8 N across the simulated friction range; see fidelity). It cannot be reopened by hand.
(4) Practice injection pad, fixed: silicone skin pad 100 x 100 x 20 mm, centre (0.230, 0.128), top 20 mm above the table. It is the injection site that was just used; no puncture is simulated.
(5) Sharps tray, free: red polypropylene open-top tray 110 (x) x 160 (y) x 60 mm high, 3 mm walls and floor (inside 104 x 154 mm), 0.35 kg, centre (0.130, -0.225).
Friction (static/dynamic): barrel 0.6/0.5, sheath 0.4/0.3, catch 0.15/0.12, pad 0.8/0.7, tray 0.6/0.5. Both arms start at their ready pose; the left gripper's centre point is more than 300 mm from the needle. Full collider table in the README.
scoring:
Measured on the syringe (pose, sheath angle, catch position), the tray and each gripper's centre point (the point midway between its finger pads) and finger opening. LOCKED means the sheath is no more than 1.5 deg short of closed (it may sit up to 3 deg past closed, on its stop) and the catch is back out to within 0.3 mm of its rest (it has dropped behind the needle); a sheath that only rests on the needle with the catch still lifted is not locked. BARE means not locked.
Sticky zero for the whole trial, checked every step: (a) while the needle is bare, any gripper other than the holding one has its centre point within 100 mm of the needle tip (the holding gripper is the one nearest the middle of the barrel); (b) while the needle is bare, the holding gripper's centre point is within 100 mm of the needle tip but not alongside the barrel (measured along the syringe, more than 5 mm beyond the barrel's shoulder or flange): it came at the hub or needle; (c) the bare needle tip touches the pad or a tray wall (tip inside the body, 1.5 mm tolerance); (d) the barrel axis drops more than 20 mm below the table top (it fell off); (e) at the moment the sheath locks, it is not being pressed on the table: its lowest point is more than 3 mm above the table top, or the needle tip is within 10 mm of the pad or of the tray's outline seen from above, or a gripper finger could be on it (a centre point closer to the sheath's bounding box than 15 mm plus half that gripper's finger opening).
Otherwise the score is read from the resting end state. Every credit needs the syringe released by both grippers (each centre point at least 30 mm from the syringe's bounding box) and syringe and tray at rest (under 0.5 mm and 0.25 deg of sheath angle per 50 ms step), held for 1 s; a syringe still held, or still moving, scores 0. Tiers (not cumulative): 1.0 = locked, the needle tip inside the channel at least 3 mm from the sheath's far end, and the syringe in the tray (all of it inside the tray's inner outline seen from above, 2 mm tolerance, lowest point below the rim, tray upright on the table). 0.4 = locked and covered the same way, resting anywhere else. 0.15 = bare but in the tray. 0.10 = bare, not in the tray, sheath swung to within 45 deg of closed. 0 = anything else, including the untouched start. Success = 1.0 held 1 s.
Real trial: use a real unit with the cannula tip ground blunt (the catch grips the shaft, so the sheath still locks), behind the cell's guard. Sticky rules (a) and (b) are read from two synchronised videos, overhead and from the side, each with a 100 mm scale bar in view: the distance from each gripper's centre point to the needle tip is taken from both views together (3D), frame by frame while the needle is bare; (c) by ink on the needle tip marking what it touched; (e) from a side video of the click. After the run: pull the sheath's far end open with a 3 N spring scale (it must not reopen), check with a ruler that the needle tip is at least 3 mm inside, and photograph the tray from above.
run_limit: 1,400 steps (70 s at 20 Hz); the scripted demo takes 28 s
reset_notes: Use a fresh syringe and needle (the lock is permanent): sheath pulled back to its 100 deg ready position, plunger pushed in, laid on its mark with the sheath level and toward the robot. Pad and tray back on their outlines.
fidelity: The maker publishes no sheath sizes or forces. Sizes are scaled from product photos against the 25 mm needle; the 3 N click (band 3 to 6 N) and the hinge friction are estimates. Check a real unit with calipers and by pressing the sheath end on a scale until it clicks. The catch is a rigid sprung plunger (real: a moulded hook). The needle is rigid; its collider is a 0.5 mm square rod. Pad rigid, no puncture or fluid. An open tray stands in for a sharps container. Nurses usually shield by thumb.
